questions.q: Which of these is the best definition of a distributed system?
options: A single powerful computer with many CPU cores
A collection of independent computers that coordinate over a network to appear as one coherent system
Any software that runs on a cloud provider
A backup server that takes over only when the primary fails
questions.explain: A distributed system is made of independent machines — each with its own memory and clock — that cooperate over a network so users experience them as a single system.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three main reasons given for building distributed systems?
options: Scaling beyond what one machine can handle
Geographic distribution closer to users
Fault isolation so one failure doesn't take everything down
Making the system easier to debug than a single machine
questions.explain: Scale, geography, and fault isolation are the three reasons covered. Distributed systems are actually harder to debug than a single machine, not easier.

questions.q: What does 'partial failure' mean in a distributed system?
options: The entire system crashes at once, like a single-machine program
Some machines in the system fail while others continue running correctly
A failure that only affects test environments, never production
A network fallacy about bandwidth
questions.explain: Partial failure means some nodes can go down while the rest of the system keeps operating — a state that doesn't exist on a single machine, where failure is all-or-nothing.

questions.q: A developer assumes a network call to another service will always succeed instantly with no data limits. Which fallacies of distributed computing is this developer ignoring?
options: Only that latency is zero
Only that bandwidth is infinite
That the network is reliable, that latency is zero, and that bandwidth is infinite
None — these are safe assumptions on modern networks
questions.explain: Assuming a call always succeeds instantly with no limits ignores all three classic fallacies: reliable network, zero latency, and infinite bandwidth.

questions.q: Why can't one machine in a distributed system simply read another machine's variables directly?
options: Because programming languages don't allow variables to have the same name on two machines
Because there is no shared memory between independent machines — they must communicate by sending messages over the network
Because only cloud providers allow memory sharing, not on-premises servers
Because variables are encrypted on every machine by default
questions.explain: Independent machines don't share memory. Any value one machine needs from another has to be sent explicitly as a message over the network.
